_comment: EV6: every civilian building, composed from the Medieval Village MegaKit (D24 -- the one architectural family). Each prefab is a recipe: modules in LOCAL metres (origin = footprint centre at ground level, front = +z), assembled once by scripts/world/building_prefabs.gd and duplicated per placement. The kit is authored at real scale on a 2m wall grid (walls 2.0w x 3.12h, measured); no scale corrections anywhere. ALL TUNABLE.
_comment_vocabulary: Bible sec12's material grade: pale plaster + warm timber for homes, uneven stone for working buildings, ONE roof family (round terracotta tiles) across the whole settlement -- the old three-family mess (BLOCKED.md, resolved by D24) is exactly what a second roof material would reinvite. Gable fronts face the viewer's approach; chimneys break the ridge line; every building sits on a low RockTrim border skirt so it meets the grass in stone, not in a hard plaster line (bible secE).
_comment_colliders: A prefab with no `colliders` gets one combined-AABB box from the placer, same as the old farm pack. The workshop authors its own so the open arch bay is genuinely enterable -- an open doorway with an invisible wall across it is the hologram village.gd's own header warns about, from the other side.

well._why_retint: round 3 (EV6-remainder-well-rocktrim-shadow): rounds 1-2 kept pushing the colour multiply warmer and it kept not closing the gap, because colour was never the real defect -- MI_RockTrim imports with metallic=1.0 (confirmed via tools/_probe_rocktrim_material.gd), a bare-metal value no stone surface wants, versus the adjacent paving's MI_UnevenBrick at a correct metallic=0.0. Under the Compatibility renderer's realtime-only lighting (no reflection probes), a full-metal surface has almost no diffuse ambient response, so it goes flat and cold in shadow while a dielectric neighbour in the identical shadow reads normally warm -- exactly the asymmetry the round-2 critic named. Fixed at the actual layer: metallic forced to 0.0 through a new optional key on the retint schema (building_prefabs.gd::_apply_retint), keeping round 2's warm colour rather than reverting it.

farmhouse_shell._why: EV6 follow-up: Grandpa's house rebuilt from the SAME kit modules as the rest of the settlement, replacing the reskinned primitive shell a blind critic still read as 'an asset from a different pack' (smooth stucco, pinstripe quoining, punched windows, shallow flat-tile roof). Two-storey: uneven-brick ground course, plaster/timber-grid upper course, kit lattice windows, the family's one round-tile roof, brick gable fronts -- the big sibling that bridges cottage_b (stone) and cottage_a (plaster/timber). Footprint 6m (x) by 10m (z), front = +z where the door is; grandpa_house.gd rotates the instance so the front gable faces the village square, and keeps interior floors, loft, stairs, furniture, markers and ALL collision itself -- this recipe deliberately authors no colliders because the house's door gate and enterable interior need collision the placer's AABB fallback would get wrong.

castle._why: OF4-rebuild (D28): landmark.gd's procedural-primitive silhouette retired in favour of a real assembled fortress, composed from BG2's Quaternius Modular Medieval Building Pack (assets/buildings/quaternius_castle -- OBJ+MTL, CC0, same publisher/art language as the Medieval Village MegaKit this file already draws from, D24's one-village-family rule treated as a fortification extension of it per BG2's own note). South wall (z=-8.448) faces the two viewpoints the site is actually seen from now that OF13 moved it out of sight of the village square and Rise path (capture_wayfinding.gd's silhouette-close/silhouette-approach, both looking north from due south with no rotation on landmark.gd's own placement) -- the gate and the tallest keep tower both sit on that face. Two courses (Wall+TallWall family) on every run for real height; a mixed set of towers (2.02m gatehouse flankers up to a 6.20m stacked keep) so the skyline is not one part repeated. landmark.gd places this prefab on a stone plinth that absorbs the site's own measured ~1.5m of local terrain relief -- every module's own y=0 here means the plinth's own top, not raw ground.
castle._why_course_seam: OF4-gate-arch (2026-08-13): the upper course sits at y=1.408, not the 1.549 OF4-rebuild shipped. 1.549 is WallBricks' full height INCLUDING its crenellations, and every wall variant in this kit is crenellated -- so stacking a second course on the first left the lower course's crenel notches (that module is solid to y=1.408 and open from 1.408 to 1.563) as a continuous row of daylight slots punched straight through the curtain at mid-height: in the gate-side frames it read as a dotted bright line running the whole wall, and again on the far wall seen through the gate itself. Seating the upper course at 1.408 buries those notches behind it. Costs 0.14m of wall height (3.90m -> 3.76m) and turns the lower parapet into a proud string course, which is what a two-course curtain wants to look like anyway.
castle._why_retint: every material in the kit's own MTLs (LightRock/DarkRock/Black/Celing/LightWood/Banner, all variants) exports at the same placeholder grey Kd (0.64,0.64,0.64) -- a real gap in this particular pack's Blender export, confirmed directly against the OBJ/MTL text, not a design choice. Retint gives each material-name slot the stone/timber/iron/heraldic tone its name implies, the same surface-name convention village.gd's own retint (MI_WindowGlass above) already uses.

modules._why: south wall (faces the camera at both viewpoints the site is seen from), two courses

THE GATE -- one module, one arch, full curtain height. OF4-gate-arch (2026-08-13) replaced the stacked WallEntranceBricks(y=0)+TallWallEntrance(y=1.549) pair that OF4-rebuild shipped here. Direct polygon measurement of both OBJs (not the vertex-bounds measurement round 3 made, which only compared bounding boxes) shows the two modules carry the SAME arch profile -- identical 15-gon outer plate, opening x=+-0.445, springing at y=0.21, apex y=0.98 -- so they were never a profile mismatch. They are two ALTERNATIVE doorway walls, each with its own complete self-contained arch at its own base. Stacked, they cut TWO separate 0.98m arches into the wall 1.549m apart with a solid band between them, which is what read as a jagged/broken opening; the differing bounding-box z (WallEntranceBricks' whole mesh is authored 0.153m off-origin in z) additionally set the lower arch 0.212m proud of the upper one, so the two holes did not even sit in the same plane. Fix: use ONE module for the whole gate bay, uniformly scaled 1.72 so it stands 4.04m (its own authored 2.347m x 1.72) against the 3.90m two-course curtain either side -- a single clean arch 1.53m wide x 1.69m tall, and a gate block that rises just above the parapet the way a gatehouse should. Uniform, not stretched: this module is the kit's PLAIN wall variant (no brick relief -- its Bricks-variant siblings have it, TallWallEntrance does not), so scaling it changes no surface detail. The scaled block's cross-section (z -0.316..0.413) fully contains the neighbouring bays' (z -0.243..0.316) where its extra 0.54m of width overlaps them, so the overlap is swallowed rather than z-fighting, and 1.72 rather than 1.662 (which would be exactly curtain height) specifically so the gate's top face is NOT coplanar with the neighbours' merlon tops. Round 4's dead end (drop to a single-course opening) is not repeated here: this is a single course that is taller than the wall, not shorter than it.

the gate passage's inner ring -- a second copy of the gate module 0.618m behind the first (a 0.014m overlap rather than an abutment, so no coplanar faces z-fight and no daylight line opens between them). OF4-gate-arch round 1: a blind critic looking at the single-ring version said the opening 'reads as bricked up ... a hole cut in one wall revealing a second wall', because a one-module-thick cut is 0.63m deep and shows the sunlit courtyard and the far curtain's inner face straight through at almost the same value as the wall around it. Two rings give the arch a 1.25m reveal with its own self-shadowed soffit and jambs, which is what makes an opening read as a passage instead of a panel. landmark.gd::_build_gate_shadow closes the far end of it.

south_bridge._why: SC14, spec 3 Gate 1. The same timber-deck-on-stone-abutments language as `footbridge` above (bible sec12), stretched to carry the south gully's 14m clear span instead of a 0.7m stream channel: seven deck slabs from -7 to +7, a stone landing on each rim at +-8, and the kit's exterior border capping each approach. Nothing new -- every module is one the settlement already stands on (D24, one village family). scripts/world/south_bridge.gd owns where it sits, what height it sits at and the gate across it; this is only the span. Deliberately NOT a scaled copy of `footbridge`: a prefab scaled 2.3x would scale its plank thickness and rail height with it, and the result reads as a toy bridge photographed close up.

quarry_foundation._why: SD16, spec §3 Band 2's 'old foundations'. A building the meadow has taken back: a brick floor, one long wall course and two stub returns, all of them the SAME `Wall_UnevenBrick_Straight` the village's own cottages are built from (D24) but SUNK so only the bottom metre stands. That is the whole trick and it is deliberate -- a ruin drawn from the same family as the living buildings is what makes the quarry read as older than the village rather than as a different game's asset pack. Vines on the standing course, brick rubble where the rest of it went.
quarry_foundation._comment_sink: The kit's walls are 3.12m tall with their origin at the base, so y = -2.1 leaves ~1.0m proud and y = -2.45 leaves ~0.67m. Sinking rather than modelling a broken top edge: the kit ships no ruined pieces, and a wall cut off by the ground plane reads as a buried course, which is what an old foundation IS.
